subject: Request: Streaming first-token SLA carveout for preemptible worker pools
messages:
From: Alex Reilly <alex.reilly@cloudfin.com>
To: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Shah <priya@bankwave.io>
Date: Thu, 05 Jul 2028 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Streaming SLA question for CloudFin PoC

Hi Vanessa,

Quick question from our performance team while we finalize the pilot: CloudFin intends to run the PoC on a cost-optimized stage that uses preemptible GPU pools for saving unit cost. The security and procurement review referenced Redwood's streaming SLA (time-to-first-token and token/sec expectations).

Our engineers observed occasional spikes in time-to-first-token (TTFT) during worker preemption/handovers — this looks correlated to node reboots and KV cache rebuilds. Before we sign the SOW, we need a clear statement about whether those preemptible pools are covered by the standard streaming SLA (i.e., TTFT 95th < 200ms and sustained 60 tokens/s). If not, what carveouts or corrective credits would Redwood propose?

Can you point me to the expected behavior and propose an exception/process if we choose to keep preemptible capacity to control cost?

Thanks,
Alex

Alex Reilly
Head of Platform Engineering, CloudFin
alex.reilly@cloudfin.com
+1 (415) 555-0189
From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>
To: Alex Reilly <alex.reilly@cloudfin.com>
Cc: Priya Shah <priya@bankwave.io]>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 05 Jul 2028 10:04:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Streaming SLA question for CloudFin PoC

Hi Alex — thanks for flagging this, helpful detail. Short answer: preemptible (spot) worker pools introduce a class of transient availability and cache-warmth variance that prevents us from committing to our standard streaming TTFT targets for requests routed to those pools.

That said, we can offer a formal carveout and clear operational controls so CloudFin can still use cost-optimized capacity with predictable expectations. Proposed outline: 
- Scope: carveout applies only to streaming endpoints served from preemptible pools (customer-visible routing tag: pool=spot).
- Measurement: TTFT guarantees and token/sec SLOs will be measured on requests served by non-spot (reserved/dedicated) capacity. For spot-served traffic we will provide separate metrics and an exception window.
- Exception policy: Redwood will exclude preemption-induced latencies from TTFT uptime calculations if the cause is a node preemption event (identified via internal preemption logs and trace correlation). We will publish the preemption windows as part of the monthly SLA report.
- Compensation: if preemption-related outages exceed X hours/month above threshold, Redwood will provide pro-rated service credits (proposal attached).

I want to loop in engineering to confirm telemetry and practical thresholds — @Marissa, @Ben, can you confirm what we can detect and how quickly we can failover to sync endpoints or reserved capacity?

Vanessa

Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Strategic Accounts — Redwood Inference

Date: Thu, 05 Jul 2028 11:22:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Streaming SLA question for CloudFin PoC

On Thu, Jul 5, 2028 at 10:04 AM Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com> wrote:
> I want to loop in engineering to confirm telemetry and practical thresholds — @Marissa, @Ben, can you confirm what we can detect and how quickly we can failover to sync endpoints or reserved capacity?

Hi all — quick engineering note with what we can realistically provide from the runtime side: 

What we can detect
- Node preemption events (host-level signal) within ~2s via CTRL plane events.
- KV-cache rebuilds are observable via trace spans; we can attribute spikes to cache-warmth vs model load.
- Request routing tags: we can label requests served by spot pools (pool=spot) and record TTFT, first-byte, and token throughput per request.

What we can do
- Failover behavior: when preemption occurs we can either (A) reassign queued requests to reserved pools (adds ~150-400ms depending on queue depth) or (B) convert streaming requests to sync (non-streaming) endpoints where the runtime returns a complete response when generation completes (adds deterministic latency but preserves throughput stability). Failover mode is configurable per-route.
- Warmth mitigation: maintain a small pinned hot-set of GPUs (buffer) for models with heavy KV-cache costs; this reduces TTFT variance but increases cost.

Suggested contract language (draft):
"For routes configured to serve traffic from preemptible worker pools, Redwood will provide operational telemetry and monthly preemption reports. TTFT and streaming-token rate SLAs will explicitly exclude preemption windows identified in Redwood's preemption logs. Redwood will offer configuration options to (i) route traffic to reserved capacity, (ii) degrade requests to the sync endpoint, or (iii) enable a small hot-buffer of pinned GPUs for reduced variance. If the customer elects to use preemptible capacity and experiences preemption-related SLA impacts beyond the agreed threshold, Redwood will provide credits as defined in the attached impact matrix."

I'll attach sample traces and the impact matrix for the legal/procurement teams to review.

Marissa

Marissa Cole
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime — Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Alex Reilly <alex.reilly@cloudfin.com>
Date: Fri, 06 Jul 2028 09:37:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Streaming SLA question for CloudFin PoC

Vanessa / team — adding a few concrete numbers we can commit to for a PoC carveout to make it actionable for procurement. These are configurable per-route: 
- Reserved baseline (recommended): 95th TTFT < 180ms, sustained token rate >= 65 tokens/s.
- Spot-served streaming (carveout): best-effort TTFT; measured TTFT for spot requests will be reported separately. For billing/SLA purposes Redwood will exclude preemption windows where >10% of capacity for that route experienced host preemption within a 60s window.
- Fallback option A (route-to-sync): when preemption is detected we can convert streaming sessions to sync with guaranteed completion latency SLO (95th < 2s for models <= 1k tokens) — useful for UX-tolerant workflows.
- Fallback option B (fast-reserve failover): reassign to reserved nodes; expected extra latency 150–400ms; lower chance of token-rate degradation.

Compensation model (PoC proposal): if preemption-caused service degradation exceeds 3 hours/month beyond a baseline allowance, Redwood will issue a credit equal to 5% of that month's service invoice for the impacted route, up to a 50% cap.

If CloudFin wants stronger TTFT guarantees while using spot capacity, the practical path is a hybrid: reserve a small hot-buffer (we recommend 3–5 pinned GPUs depending on model size) and send latency-sensitive sessions there while routing batch/high-throughput sessions to spot pools. This preserves the cost advantage while giving a measurable TTFT baseline.

Ben

Ben Carter
Head of Product — Serving Runtime, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com
From: Alex Reilly <alex.reilly@cloudfin.com>

Date: Mon, 07 Jul 2028 16:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Streaming SLA question for CloudFin PoC

Vanessa / team — thanks, that level of detail is exactly what procurement needs. We prefer fallback option A (route-to-sync) for the initial pilot because some of our client-facing flows tolerate a single-result response better than visible streaming jitter. Two follow-ups from our side: 
1) Can you provide the exact DocuSign amendment language for the carveout and the credit schedule (we need something legal can attach to the SOW)?
2) For demo day next week, can Marissa share a short trace and a one-slide summary of the failover latency profile so we can show engineering and product?

If we get the amendment and the slide by EOD Wednesday we can proceed with signatures.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.
Alex
